summary: Specifies the syntax of Netnews articles within the Internet Message Format and MIME. It updates the specification to reflect current practice and incorporates incremental changes from other documents. It obsoletes RFC 1036.

plainLanguage.summary: Netnews is an old discussion system where people post public messages. This note defines how each post is laid out, such as its header lines and body.

subtitle: The header rules every Netnews post must follow, built on top of Internet email format and MIME.

tldr.problem: Netnews servers exchange articles with each other, but the older article standard no longer matched current practice, and news software needs stricter, faster-to-parse headers than ordinary email.
tldr.mechanism: An article is an Internet Message Format message with extra restrictions: six mandatory header fields (Date, From, Message-ID, Newsgroups, Path, Subject), a set of optional news-specific fields, and MIME for non-ASCII text and attachments.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5536 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1036 and RFC 1849. It defines only the article syntax; the architecture and protocol rules live in the companion RFC 5537.

today: RFC 5536 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1036 and RFC 1849, and it is meant to be read together with RFC 5537.

sections.title: What Netnews Articles Are
sections.content:
Netnews is a set of protocols for generating, storing and retrieving news articles and for exchanging them among a widely spread readership. It is organized around newsgroups, and the protocols most commonly use a flooding algorithm that propagates copies throughout a network of participating servers. Typically only one copy is stored per server.

RFC 5536 specifies the syntax of those articles in the context of the Internet Message Format (RFC 5322) and MIME (RFC 2045). It obsoletes RFC 1036 (the unit metadata also lists RFC 1849) to reflect current practice. It is the first of a set of documents that replace RFC 1036; RFC 5537 covers the protocol issues independent of transports such as NNTP (RFC 3977).

The RFC defines what article content is passed between systems. How a server stores articles locally is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Netnews is a big shared message board where many computers keep copies of the same posts. This document describes what each post must look like when computers pass it along.

sections.title: Key Terms: Articles, Groups and Agents
sections.content:
An article is the unit of Netnews, analogous to an email message. A proto-article has not yet been injected into the news system and may lack some mandatory header fields. A message identifier distinguishes an article from every other article ever posted anywhere, and articles with the same identifier are treated as the same article whatever their bodies say.

A newsgroup is a named forum for a specific topic. An article posted to several groups is crossposted, which differs from posting separate copies. A group may be moderated, so submissions are mailed to a moderator instead of being posted directly. A followup responds to an earlier article and always carries a References header field naming it.

The RFC uses agent for both user agents (software that helps people post and read) and news servers. An agent generates a construct it creates and accepts one that another entity created without treating it as an error. Many MUST rules apply to generating, while accepting is usually more lenient.
sections.plainLanguage: A post is like a letter with a one-of-a-kind serial number. Letters go on topic boards, and a reply points back to the letter it answers.

sections.title: Format Rules Built on Email
sections.content:
An article is conformant if it follows Section 3 of RFC 5322 plus the extra rules in this RFC. Obsolete email syntax is not allowed, with two exceptions that must be accepted: the obs-phrase construct (agents MUST NOT generate it) and the GMT time zone. Agents MUST generate only conformant articles.

The Netnews grammar is a strict subset of the email grammar, so every article is also valid email format, but the reverse is not guaranteed. General rules for all header fields include:

  • At least one space MUST follow the colon after a header field name.
  • Every line of a header field body MUST contain at least one non-whitespace character, so no header field body can be empty.
  • Agents MUST NOT generate header field lines longer than 998 octets, though they MAY accept them. Folding lets a field exceed this in total.
  • Header fields are US-ASCII. Other characters MUST be encoded with MIME mechanisms (RFC 2047 and RFC 2231).

User agents MUST meet the MIME conformance definition of RFC 2049 and MUST support RFC 2231. This gives international text and multimedia bodies, and encoded words in any unstructured header field.
sections.plainLanguage: A post is a normal email-style letter with stricter rules. Every header line must say something, the lines cannot be too long, and fancy letters must be written in a special code.

sections.title: The Six Mandatory Header Fields
sections.content:
Every conformant article MUST have exactly one each of Date, From, Message-ID, Newsgroups, Path and Subject. Each of the news fields defined here MUST NOT occur more than once.

Date, From and Subject are the same as in RFC 5322, plus the general restrictions. Agents MUST accept the deprecated GMT zone in dates.

Message-ID is stricter than email. The identifier is <id-left@id-right>, MUST NOT exceed 250 octets, allows no comments, and cannot contain > or whitespace. The id-right part is case-sensitive, so a simple octet comparison always decides whether two identifiers match. Implementations SHOULD use a domain name as id-right.

Newsgroups lists groups as dot-separated components. Optional folding in the list SHOULD NOT be generated but MUST be accepted. Components SHOULD NOT be all digits or contain uppercase. Names beginning with _ are reserved for future standards, names beginning with a plus sign or a hyphen are for private use, and example.* and poster are reserved and MUST NOT name a group.

Path records the route since injection. Each agent that processes an article prepends at least one identity, so servers avoid sending articles to sites that already have them. A !! means the agent on the left verified the identity on the right. The tail entry is historically the sender and is often the string not-for-mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Every post needs six labels: when it was written, who wrote it, its own ID, which boards it goes on, which computers it passed through, and what it is about. Each post gets just one of each.

sections.title: Optional Header Fields
sections.content:
Optional fields add behavior but are not required in every article. Some are required for certain article types, as discussed in RFC 5537.

  • Followup-To asks where replies should go. It SHOULD NOT appear unless it differs from Newsgroups. The keyword poster asks that replies be emailed to the author instead.
  • Distribution limits propagation. world is the default and SHOULD NOT be written out, and local means the local site only. All MUST NOT be used.
  • Control marks a control message and an article with it MUST NOT also have Supersedes. Supersedes names one message identifier and acts like a cancel followed by the new article.
  • Approved shows who approved the post, mainly for moderated groups and control messages. Expires, Archive (yes or no), Organization, Summary and References carry the poster's wishes and context.
  • Injection-Date MUST be inserted whenever an article is injected and lets servers judge staleness with a server-added time. Agents MUST NOT alter an existing Date when adding it.
  • User-Agent names the posting software, and Xref says where the last server filed the article.

Injection-Info records how the article entered the system. Its parameters are posting-host, posting-account, logging-data and mail-complaints-to. Some of this has privacy implications, and posting-account SHOULD be given in a form other sites cannot interpret.
sections.plainLanguage: Extra labels are like sticky notes: where replies should go, how far the post may travel, when it goes stale, and a stamp from the first post office showing where it came from.

sections.title: Obsolete Fields and Changes from RFC 1036
sections.content:
The header fields Date-Received, Posting-Version and Relay-Version (from RFC 850) and Also-Control, Article-Names, Article-Updates and See-Also (from Son of 1036) are declared obsolete. They MUST NOT be generated and SHOULD be ignored. Lines, once used by NNTP overview, is obsolescent: agents SHOULD ignore it and SHOULD NOT generate it.

Appendix B lists what changed from RFC 1036. Comments are supported in the newly defined fields and those inherited from email, but still not in Control, Distribution, Followup-To, Lines, Message-ID, Newsgroups, Path, Supersedes and Xref. Multiple addresses are allowed in From, whitespace folding is permitted in Newsgroups, Path got a richer syntax, and MIME became an integral part of Netnews. New fields include Injection-Date, Archive, Injection-Info and User-Agent. The old convention of treating subjects starting with cmsg as control messages was removed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old labels are retired like worn-out stamps. New labels were added, and posts can now carry any language or picture.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The article format provides no confidentiality, sender authentication or non-repudiation. Such services must be layered above it with protocols like S/MIME or PGP/MIME, or below it with secure versions of news transport protocols.

Message identifiers must be unique, and a server may refuse a transfer if it has already seen the identifier. An attacker who can predict an identifier could post its own article with that identifier first and block the real one from propagating. Agents that generate identifiers SHOULD therefore make them unpredictable.

The RFC also warns that the full range of MIME parameter encodings allows constructs that simple parsers may misread, and such parsing deficiencies may be used in an attack. Further considerations are in RFC 5537.
sections.plainLanguage: The label format has no lock. If someone can guess a post's serial number, they can sneak in a fake post with the same number first, so numbers should be hard to guess.

viz.caption: THE SIX MANDATORY HEADER FIELDS (RFC 5536 SECTION 3.1)

items.title: Date
items.text: Same as email; GMT zone must be accepted.

items.title: Message-ID
items.text: Unique, at most 250 octets, no comments.

items.title: Newsgroups
items.text: Dot-separated group names the article is posted to.

items.title: Path
items.text: Route taken since injection, newest agent first.

items.label: Host
items.desc: FQDN and/or IP address of the host the news server received the article from.

items.label: Account
items.desc: Source of the article in a form the server administrator can interpret.

items.label: Logging data
items.desc: Typically a session number to find the origin in server logs.

items.label: Complaints
items.desc: Mailboxes for complaints about the poster.
